headline: Multiphase pipelines carry the hardest integrity problem in the Gulf's gas build-out
deck: Gas, condensate and water moving together in one line produce corrosion, vibration and slugging that a single-phase line never sees.
excerpt: Pipelines are the fourth class at STATIC Arabia, and the multiphase lines feeding Saudi Arabia's gas expansion are the most demanding of them. Everything downstream, including the slug catchers now being built in the Kingdom, exists to manage what they deliver.
content:
A pipeline carrying a single, clean, dry phase is a well-understood asset with predictable degradation. A pipeline carrying gas, condensate and produced water together is a different engineering problem, and it is the one the Gulf's gas expansion has been adding at scale.

Multiphase flow does not behave as a uniform mixture. Depending on flow rate, pipe inclination and the ratio of phases, the fluids arrange themselves into regimes — stratified, wavy, annular, slug — and the regime determines what the pipe experiences. In slug flow, liquid accumulates and is pushed along in intermittent masses, which loads the pipe mechanically at bends and supports, and delivers surges to whatever is at the far end.

That is why slug catchers exist, and why they are built at the scale they are. Zamil Steel recently delivered two gas slug catcher and separator units for Package 4 of Aramco's Fadhili Gas Increment Project, each 44 metres long and around 1,750 tonnes, with 196mm walls clad in Alloy 825. Those dimensions are a direct expression of the surge volumes a multiphase line can produce.

The integrity problems compound. Water in the line, combined with carbon dioxide or hydrogen sulphide, creates internal corrosion that concentrates where water collects — at low points, on the bottom of the pipe, downstream of bends. That is a different inspection target from general wall loss, and it is why intelligent pigging runs on these lines are analysed for localised metal loss rather than average thickness.

Flow-induced vibration is the other mechanism, and it is one the industry has taken more seriously over the past decade. High-velocity multiphase flow excites piping systems, and the damage appears not in the main line but in the small-bore connections welded to it — instrument tappings, drains, vents — where a fatigue crack can develop in service without any loss of wall thickness anywhere else. Screening methodologies for acoustic and flow-induced vibration have become a standard part of design review for exactly this reason.

The material selection question follows. Carbon steel with corrosion inhibitor injection is the economical answer and depends on the inhibitor reaching the right places continuously. Corrosion-resistant alloy cladding removes that dependency at considerable capital cost, which is the trade-off visible in the Fadhili vessels' 196mm carbon steel wall with 3.2mm of Alloy 825 on the inside.

For the Kingdom's fabrication base, this class of work is the demanding end of what it now does. Aramco's in-Kingdom total value add programme crossed 70 per cent local content in February 2026 and now targets 75 per cent by 2030, and the equipment at issue here is precisely the category where that percentage is hardest to move.

STATIC Arabia runs at Dhahran Expo until 10 September.
